summary: This informational RFC defines an extension to BCP 47 language tags, introduced by the singleton letter t. It lets a tag describe the source language or script of content that was transliterated, transcribed, translated, or otherwise derived from something else, plus some extra identifying information. It is not on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A label for a language usually says what language you are reading. This adds a note saying what language the text came from before it was changed, like writing on a translated book which language the original was in.

questions: how to mark transliterated text language
subtitle: Language tag extension for specifying the source of transformed content.

tldr.problem: Language tags (BCP 47) identify what language content is in, but they cannot describe the source when content has been transliterated, transcribed, translated or otherwise transformed from another language.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6497 defines the 't' extension to BCP 47, which adds subtags after the source language to indicate transformations. For example, 'ja-t-it' means Japanese content transformed from Italian, and 'und-Cyrl-t-und-latn-m0-ungegn' means Cyrillic transformed from Latin according to the UNGEGN standard.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now tag transformed content with both its target language and its source, enabling translation memories, speech recognizers tuned for specific accents, and proper handling of transliteration standards in applications like maps and data processing.

today: RFC 6497 remains the active specification for the 't' extension to BCP 47 language tags. The extension is maintained by the Unicode Consortium through the CLDR project. Applications including translation management systems, speech recognition platforms, and localization tools use this extension to track the source language of transformed content.

sections.title: The Problem of Transformed Content
sections.content:
BCP 47 defines language tags that identify the language of content (e.g., ja for Japanese, en for English). However, they cannot describe transformations. Consider a map that shows Russian city names written in Japanese characters (katakana). The content is in Japanese, but the correct transliteration depends on knowing it came from Russian.

Transliterations vary by source, target, and transformation rules. For example, the Russian name Путин (Putin) becomes "Putin" when transliterated to English but "Poutine" when transliterated to French. Different organizations (UNGEGN, Library of Congress, ISO) have different transliteration standards.

Without a way to tag the source language, systems cannot:

  • Apply the correct transliteration rules
  • Build translation memories that track what language the source was
  • Configure speech recognizers for non-native speakers (e.g., English spoken with a Chinese accent)
  • Handle localization workflows that need to distinguish content versions

RFC 6497 solves this by extending language tags with source information.
sections.eli5: When you translate a book or write a city name in a different alphabet, you need to remember where it came from. This lets you tag that information in the language label.

sections.title: The 't' Extension and Structure
sections.content:
The 't' extension is introduced by the letter 't' as a singleton (a single-character subtag) followed by source language subtags. For example:

  • ja-t-it: Japanese, source Italian
  • ja-Kana-t-it: Japanese Katakana, source Italian
  • und-Latn-t-und-cyrl: Latin script, source Cyrillic script

The source language tag after 't' is a regular BCP 47 language tag (language, script, region, variants). When only the script is relevant, the language uses und (undetermined).

After the source, the extension may optionally include fields that provide additional transformation metadata. Fields are separated by two-character codes like m0 (for transformation mechanism). The first field currently defined is m0, which specifies the transliteration or transcription standard used.

Examples of mechanism fields:

  • ja-t-it-m0-ungegn: Japanese from Italian using UNGEGN standard
  • und-Cyrl-t-und-latn-m0-ungegn-2007: Cyrillic to Latin using UNGEGN version 2007

The field separators (like m0) are always letters followed by digits, so they cannot conflict with language subtags. This ensures that regular BCP 47 parsers will recognize them as separate extensions.
sections.eli5: You write the target language, then a 't', then the source language, then optionally the rules used to transform it. Each part is just letters and numbers separated by hyphens.

sections.title: Scope and Not Intended for
sections.content:
The 't' extension is intended for use when a content item is tagged with a single transformed language. It is NOT intended for structured data that already has separate source and target identifiers. For example, in a localization interchange format like XLIFF, the source and target languages are already separate fields, so using ja-t-it for the target language would be redundant and confusing.

Conversely, when a single content piece has undergone transformation (a scanned document transliterated into digital form, a set of city names transliterated for a map), the 't' extension is the right way to tag it. This includes informal transformations (not just formal standards) such as text for second-language speech recognition.

The extension is also useful in queries: a user or application can request content with a tag like ja-t-it-m0-ungegn to ask for Japanese content transliterated from Italian according to the UNGEGN standard, and the system will try to return the closest match.
sections.eli5: Use this when a single piece of text is in one language but came from another. Do not use it for formats that already separately store the source and target languages.

sections.title: Mechanism Field and Versioning
sections.content:
The m0 mechanism field allows specifying a transformation standard (UNGEGN, Library of Congress, BGN, ISO, MCST, DIN, GOST). The field value is a sequence of subtags; the first subtag is the mechanism name (3-8 alphanumeric characters), and optionally a second subtag specifies a version.

Versions can be specified as dates (YYYY, YYYYMM, YYYYMMDD) for standards that are identified by release dates, or in other formats specified by Unicode Technical Standard #35 (UTS#35) for standards that use non-date versioning schemes.

Examples:

  • m0-ungegn-2007: UNGEGN standard version 2007
  • m0-bgn-199906: BGN version from June 1999
  • m0-iso-v3: ISO standard version v3

Canonicalization (converting to a standard form) requires lowercase letters for all subtags. The order of fields (m0, m1, etc.) is alphabetical in the canonical form, but the order of subtags within a field must be preserved because it is significant.
sections.eli5: You can add which exact standard was used and what year or version. Dates are written as four-digit years (2007), or year-month (199906), or year-month-day (20110623).

sections.title: Registration and Maintenance
sections.content:
The 't' extension is maintained by the Unicode Consortium, which owns the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR). New mechanism subtags and field definitions are registered through the CLDR technical committee via a ticketing system at cldr.unicode.org.

Registration proposals must include the proposed subtag name (3-8 characters), a description sufficient to distinguish it from others, and versioning information if the mechanism does not use dates. The committee must post proposals publicly within 2 weeks and respond within 4 weeks.

Field subtag assignments that can be made by successive versions of Unicode Technical Standard #35 without requiring a new RFC include:

  • Allocation of new field separators (m0, m1, etc.)
  • Allocation of subtags valid after a field separator
  • Addition of aliases and descriptions
  • Modification of descriptions

Changes to the syntax or meaning of the extension itself would require a new RFC that obsoletes RFC 6497. The stability policy ensures that once a subtag is registered, it is never withdrawn or substantially changed in meaning.

Machine-readable data files listing valid subtags are maintained in the CLDR archive at unicode.org/Public/cldr/, updated with each CLDR release. These files enable applications to validate 't' extension subtags.
sections.eli5: The Unicode Consortium keeps the list of standard transformation names. Anyone can propose a new standard by filing a ticket. The committee posts it publicly and decides within 4 weeks whether to add it.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
Some practical applications of the 't' extension:

Maps and geographic names: A map application transliterates Russian city names to Latin script for English users. The tags would be: Russian names: ru, English transliteration: en-Latn-t-ru-m0-ungegn-2007.

Voice interfaces: A speech recognition system is tuned for English speakers trying to pronounce Spanish words. The tag could be es-t-en, indicating Spanish content with training data from English speakers.

Translation management: A translation memory stores German source documents that have been translated to Spanish. Each translation entry is tagged with es-t-de to indicate the source was German.

Heritage languages: Historical Japanese texts that were written using Chinese characters (kanji) come from Chinese but are read as Japanese. The tag ja-t-zh indicates Japanese reading of Chinese-derived content.

Script conversion: An application converts Arabic script to Latin script. The tag is und-Latn-t-und-Arab, indicating Latin script sourced from Arabic, with no specific language specified.
sections.eli5: Use it for maps that show foreign city names, voice systems trained on non-native speakers, translation tools that track where text came from, and any system that needs to remember what language content came from before it was transformed.
